desc: This station involves assessing a woman at 36 weeks with reduced fetal movements and a normal CTG, explaining the result honestly, supporting her anxiety after a previous stillbirth, and answering her questions about food safety, aspirin and later health risks.
diagnosis: Reduced fetal movements with normal cardiotocograph
explain:
Reduced fetal movements

Women should be encouraged to learn their baby's usual pattern of movements and to report any reduction promptly, at any time of day or night. Assessment includes a focused history, maternal observations, assessment of fundal height or growth, and a CTG. A normal CTG is reassuring but does not exclude the risk of a poor outcome, so an ultrasound to assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid volume should be offered. Previous stillbirth, growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, diabetes and maternal supine sleeping are recognised risk factors. Women should be advised to sleep on their side. The Safer Baby Bundle supports awareness of movements, side sleeping, smoking cessation, growth surveillance and timing of birth.

Communicating after a previous stillbirth

  • Acknowledge the loss and validate the anxiety. Do not say "it will be fine".

  • Be honest about uncertainty, but promise to take her concerns seriously and to respond each time she presents.

  • Plan surveillance and the timing of birth together with the obstetric team, and offer perinatal mental health support. Screen for depression and anxiety and ask about self-harm.

TPAL

T: term births (37 weeks or more). P: preterm births (20 weeks to under 37 weeks). A: pregnancies lost before 20 weeks. L: living children. A multiple pregnancy counts once. A stillbirth at term counts as a term birth. Rachel is G3, with T1 P0 A1 L0, and her current pregnancy adds to gravidity but not to parity until she gives birth.

Listeria and food safety

Listeria is usually a mild illness in the mother but can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth or severe neonatal infection. Advise avoiding cold deli meats, pâté and soft or semi-soft cheeses such as brie and camembert, along with other high-risk foods listed in the national guidance, and give a written list. Avoidance lowers the risk but cannot remove it. Any fever or flu-like illness in pregnancy should prompt early contact with the maternity unit.

Aspirin for pre-eclampsia prevention

Low-dose aspirin (100 to 150 mg nocte) started before 16 weeks lowers the risk of pre-eclampsia in women at higher risk, such as those with previous pre-eclampsia. In line with current Australian guidance (SOMANZ 2023), it is stopped at 36 weeks, or earlier if birth is imminent. Rachel is at 36+2, so the correct advice is that it should now be stopped. Because she is unsure, the candidate should confirm the plan with the obstetric team and not simply rely on memory.

Later health risks of pre-eclampsia and gestational diabetes

  • Pregnancy acts as a cardiometabolic stress test. Both conditions predict higher later cardiovascular disease risk.

  • Pre-eclampsia also raises the later risk of chronic hypertension, stroke and chronic kidney disease.

  • Gestational diabetes greatly raises the risk of type 2 diabetes. A glucose tolerance test is recommended 6 to 12 weeks after birth, followed by glucose screening at least every 1 to 3 years.

  • The GP should continue to review blood pressure, weight, lipids and lifestyle after pregnancy.

Chorionicity and amnionicity in twins

The time of splitting of the fertilised egg determines the twin type. A split early enough to form two chorions also forms two amnions, so a monoamniotic twin pregnancy is always monochorionic. Monoamniotic dichorionic twins therefore cannot exist. Monochorionic monoamniotic twins are rare and carry a higher risk of cord entanglement, so they need close specialist monitoring.
focus: Antenatal visit: food advice, reduced fetal movements, anxiety after stillbirth and later health risks
guide:
A high-performing candidate would take a focused history that clarifies the change in movements and screens for bleeding, fluid loss, infection and pre-eclampsia symptoms. They would state her obstetric history correctly (G3, T1 P0 A1 L0) and screen mood. They would explain that the normal CTG is reassuring but not a guarantee, offer an ultrasound, and give clear advice to return at any hour if movements change. They would acknowledge the stillbirth, avoid false promises, and offer to plan monitoring and support together. They would give accurate listeria advice, recognise that aspirin should now be stopped and confirm this with the obstetric team, and explain her later cardiovascular and diabetes risks.

A borderline candidate would take a reasonable history but miss the obstetric summary or the mood screen. They might say the baby is fine because the trace is normal, or promise that everything will be all right. They might give vague food advice, tell her to keep taking aspirin, or not explain the later health risks of pre-eclampsia and gestational diabetes.
patient:
Profile:

  • Name: Rachel Bennett.

  • Age: 34-years-old.

  • Occupation: Primary school teacher (on leave).

  • Gender: Female (she/her).

  • Aboriginal/Torres Strait Islander: No.

  • Presenting location: Maternity day assessment unit.

Demeanour: Pale, tearful and tense. Sits forward, holds her abdomen and keeps checking the clock. Speaks quickly. Calms slightly if the candidate is warm and unhurried.

Opening statement: "I haven't felt the baby move much since last night. I'm so scared it's happening again."

Reduced movements (give if asked):

  • The baby is usually very active, especially after dinner and when she lies down in the evening.

  • Since about 6 pm yesterday she has felt only a few weak flutters. This morning she felt perhaps two small movements.

  • She tried a cold drink and lying on her left side. This did not help much. She felt the baby move a little during the heart rate trace.

  • She has no vaginal bleeding, no fluid leaking, no abdominal pain or tightenings, no fall or abdominal injury.

  • No fever, chills, sore throat or flu-like illness at any point in the pregnancy.

  • No headache, visual disturbance, upper abdominal pain or new swelling.

  • She sleeps on her back at times and often wakes on her back.

  • She waited about 18 hours before coming in because she did not want to "waste anyone's time". If asked, say she is sorry she did not come sooner.

Obstetric history:

  • This is her third pregnancy (G3).

  • First pregnancy: spontaneous miscarriage at 9 weeks.

  • Second pregnancy (two years ago): pre-eclampsia (high blood pressure and protein in urine) diagnosed at 37 weeks. Her baby, a boy, was stillborn at 39 weeks, before induction took place. No cause was found other than a small placenta.

  • She has no living children. If asked, she says: "I've never taken a baby home."

  • If the candidate says a TPAL or similar summary, she does not need to comment. Correct summary: 1 term birth, 0 preterm, 1 pregnancy lost before 20 weeks, 0 living children.

This pregnancy:

  • Single baby. Conceived naturally.

  • Takes aspirin 150 mg every night, started at 13 weeks because of the pre-eclampsia last time.

  • Gestational diabetes diagnosed at 27 weeks on a glucose tolerance test. Managed with diet only. Home sugar readings have been fine.

  • Growth scan at 32 weeks was normal.

  • Antenatal visits have been regular. Blood pressure has been normal this pregnancy.

Medical history: Nil other. No mental health diagnosis before the stillbirth.

Medications: Aspirin 150 mg nocte and a pregnancy multivitamin with iodine. No other medications.

Allergies: Nil known.

Social history:

  • Lives with her husband, Daniel, who is very supportive.

  • Non-smoker, no alcohol and no drugs since conceiving.

Mood (give if asked):

  • She has been very anxious since the stillbirth and sleeps poorly. She counts movements through the night.

  • She feels low at times but has no thoughts of harming herself and no plans.

  • She has not seen a counsellor or psychologist this pregnancy and would like help if offered.

Scripted responses to the candidate:

  • If told the trace is normal: "So the baby is fine? Can I go home?"

  • If the candidate says everything is fine or that the baby is definitely okay: become more distressed. "They said that last time too."

  • If the candidate explains that the trace cannot guarantee everything is fine and offers an ultrasound: accept, with relief. Ask how long it will take.

  • If the candidate does not say when to come back, ask: "What if it happens again when I get home?"

  • If the candidate uses jargon (for example CTG, liquor, EFW, OGTT, listeriosis), interrupt and ask what it means.

Questions (ask in this order as time allows):

  1. "Is it going to be all right this time? Please just tell me it will be."

  2. "Yesterday Daniel bought me a ham and brie baguette. I ate half before I remembered I'm not supposed to. What foods should I avoid, and should I be worried?" (She has no fever or flu-like symptoms now.)

  3. "I take my aspirin every night. I think the midwife said something about stopping it at some point but I can't remember. Should I keep taking it until the baby comes?" (She took her last dose last night and has not taken tonight's.)

  4. "I had pre-eclampsia last time and now sugar diabetes in this pregnancy. Does that mean anything for my health later on?"

  5. (Only if time allows) "My cousin is having twins. She says they share one sac but have two separate placentas. Is that possible?"

The candidate may ask further questions of you – use only the provided history above.

The candidate should interact with you using non-medical terminology. Please interrupt the candidate if they use medical terminology that would not be clearly understood by the lay public.
points: A normal CTG for reduced fetal movements is reassuring but not a guarantee, so offer an ultrasound and advise her to come in again straight away, at any hour, if movements change.
After a previous stillbirth, acknowledge the loss and validate the anxiety. Do not promise a good outcome, but promise to take her worries seriously and plan monitoring and support together.
TPAL records term births, preterm births, pregnancies lost before 20 weeks, and living children. A term stillbirth counts as a term birth.
Advise avoiding cold deli meats and soft cheeses because of listeria. Avoidance lowers but does not remove the risk, and a fever or flu-like illness needs prompt review.
Low-dose aspirin for pre-eclampsia prevention is stopped at 36 weeks (or earlier if birth is imminent). Confirm the plan with the obstetric team.

Pre-eclampsia and gestational diabetes both raise later cardiovascular risk. Pre-eclampsia also raises the risk of hypertension, stroke and chronic kidney disease, and gestational diabetes greatly raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, hence the postpartum glucose tolerance test and ongoing screening.

stem:
You are the junior doctor in the maternity day assessment unit of a metropolitan public hospital. Your patient is Rachel Bennett, a 34-year-old woman at 36+2 weeks of pregnancy. She presented 45 minutes ago because she has felt her baby moving less since yesterday evening.

The midwife has recorded observations and performed a 40-minute CTG. You and the registrar have reviewed the trace and it is normal (baseline 140 bpm, normal variability, accelerations present, no decelerations). The registrar has asked you to speak with Rachel while they review another patient.

  • BP: 116/72 mmHg

  • HR: 84 bpm

  • T: 36.8°C

  • RR: 16 breaths per minute

  • O2 Sats: 99% on room air

  • Urine dipstick: protein nil, glucose nil

An ultrasound slot is available in the unit today if requested. You do not need to examine Rachel.

Explain the CTG result and the next steps to Rachel, and respond to her worries (2 minutes).
